Where Valley Fever conditions line up with outdoor work

Valley Fever comes from a fungus that lives in soil in parts of California. People breathe it in when dry soil is stirred into the air. This page maps where the climate most resembles places people already get sick, and shows how many people work outdoors there.

What Valley Fever is

A fungus called Coccidioides grows in soil in dry parts of California and the Southwest. Wind, digging, driving, farming and construction all disturb that soil, and tiny spores can go into the air. Breathing them in can cause an illness called Valley Fever, or coccidioidomycosis.

Most people who breathe in the spores never feel ill. Some get something like a bad chest cold or flu that lasts weeks. A small number become seriously ill, and the infection can spread beyond the lungs. It does not pass from person to person.

The illness matters for workplace safety because the people most likely to disturb dry soil are people doing their jobs: farm work, construction, oil and gas, road work, firefighting and similar trades.

Three separate things, kept separate on this page

Where the fungus could live is not the same as when spores are in the air, and neither is the same as how many people get sick. This page never treats one as a stand-in for another.

Explore the map

Point at or tap a county to zoom in and see its numbers. Switch layers to compare reported illness, climate match, and where outdoor work is concentrated.

Read this before using the map

The climate layer does not show where the fungus has been found in the ground. Almost no one has tested California soil for it. It shows where conditions resemble places people already get sick. That relationship is correlative, things that go together, not proof that climate causes illness. Use it to decide where to look closer, never as a hazard assessment for a particular address.

Kern County carries more Valley Fever than anywhere else in California. It is also where Labor Code section 6709 training duties apply most broadly.

Why there is no map of individual cases

California publishes Valley Fever counts by county and by year. It does not publish where inside a county someone was exposed, or on what date. Nothing on this page places individual cases, because doing so would mean inventing the locations.

Who works in these places

The occupational question behind this map: how many people whose jobs disturb soil live where the climate scores highest.

About 1.65 million Californians work in agriculture, construction, mining or oil and gas, roughly 9% of everyone employed. They are not spread evenly. These come from a large sample survey, so read them as close estimates rather than exact head counts.

In the quarter of the state where the climate scores highest, outdoor industries account for 13.3% of jobs, against 7.5% everywhere else. That quarter holds 34.8% of California's outdoor workers but only 23.1% of its total workforce.

Around 8.6% of California's business establishments, about 88,000 of 1023,000, are in those same industries.

Workforce figures: American Community Survey 2018–2022, for areas of roughly 100,000 people each. Business counts: County Business Patterns 2022. Neither contains any case data. This describes who is present, not who got sick.

How we checked the map

A map that only fits the places it was built from proves nothing. So it was built with one hand tied behind its back.

The model was given case data from 2001 to 2010 only, and only from the seven counties reporting at least 20 cases per 100,000 residents in those years. It was then asked to rank the 51 counties it had never been told anything about, in years that had not happened yet.

  • Inside its learning window the map scored 0.28 on average; across the 13 later years it scored 0.25. Losing only about three hundredths means the pattern carried forward rather than fading.
  • For 2011, the first year it had never seen, the score was 0.27. Shuffling the county labels 2,000 times produced a better score only about 3 times in 100, so this is unlikely to be chance.
  • 12 of the 13 unseen years came out positive. The exception was 2021, when the map was no better than chance. Individual years are noisy; the average across many years is the more reliable guide.

What the yearly maps do and do not show

Maps for different years look very similar to each other. Climate variation appears to move how much illness is reported statewide from year to year, with wetter winters tending to be followed by more cases the following season, much more than it moves where that illness happens. The geography is stable; the volume is not.

What this map cannot tell you

  • It does not find the fungus. It compares climate. No layer here is a soil test.
  • It cannot tell you about a specific address. Each square on the map is about four kilometers across, and conditions vary within one field.
  • It does not measure dust in the air. Whether spores are actually airborne on a given day depends on wind, moisture and whether anyone is disturbing the ground.
  • Reported cases are not all cases. Many infections are never tested. Places with more testing report more illness, which can make them look worse than similar places nearby.
  • It shows association, not cause. Climate and illness travel together here. That is not the same as climate causing the illness.

What soil testing actually shows

People reasonably ask why we model climate instead of just testing the dirt. The answer is that testing soil for this fungus almost always comes back negative, even where people are getting sick.

  • A 2023 study in the San Joaquin Valley found the fungus in none of 472 samples from farmed soil, but in 89 of 238 samples from rodent burrows on undeveloped land nearby. Where you dig changes the answer completely.
  • An early California survey grew the fungus from about 4 of 720 soil samples.
  • There has never been a systematic statewide soil survey of California for it.
  • The CDC states that testing soil for Coccidioides "is currently done only for scientific research. It is not typically used to predict disease spread."

That is the gap this map is meant to help with: not to replace soil testing, but to narrow down where testing and dust controls would be worth the effort.

Where work has been linked to outbreaks

Clusters among workers have repeatedly followed soil disturbance without dust protection. Documented examples include a solar farm construction site in Monterey County (2016–17), two Central Valley prisons (2009–2013), a wildland firefighting crew digging fire lines near Tehachapi (2021), and an archaeological dig near Red Bluff (1972) where 17 of 39 students fell ill.

Technical details

How a year is defined

Predictors for a given case-year come from the 12 months ending in September of that year, plus the winter before them (October to March) and the winter before that. Nothing from after September of the year is used, so a year's estimate never uses its own late-season weather. The two-winters-back rainfall term is included because wet winters are thought to grow the fungus before a later dry season lifts it into the air.

Data sources and model

Climate: PRISM 4 km monthly rainfall and temperature, 1999–2023, giving 23 case-years built from 864 monthly grids. Cases: California Health and Human Services open data, coccidioidomycosis by county and year, 2001–2023. Workforce: American Community Survey 2018–2022. Businesses: County Business Patterns 2022. Terrain: elevation.

Method: a standard mapping technique called MaxEnt, which turns climate measurements into a score between 0 and 1 for every square on the map. A record is one 4 km grid cell in one year. Cells count as present in a year if their county reported at least 20 cases per 100,000 that year. Comparison cells are drawn from census tract centers across the whole state, so that the map reflects where conditions match rather than simply where people live.

Model performance figures

Full-period model: 7,514 presence and 20,700 comparison records; area under the curve 0.87 on training data and 0.82 when tested on geographically separated blocks it was not trained on. Agreement with county rates on the 51 counties it was never given labels for averaged 0.25 across 13 unseen years, ranging from -0.05 to 0.50. In its weakest year the map was no better than chance. Averaged across all years and compared with pooled 2001–2023 illness, agreement is 0.60 on those same counties.

Agreement here means rank agreement: whether the counties the map puts near the top are the ones that actually report the most illness. It runs from −1 to 1, where 0 means no better than chance. It describes how well the map orders counties, not how many cases it predicts. Statisticians call this measure Spearman's rank correlation.

Known weaknesses

Presence labels come from county-level rates, so every cell in a county shares one label; this blurs conditions inside large counties. Reporting has increased over the period, so any apparent strengthening over time should not be read as the fungus spreading. Coastal areas such as San Luis Obispo are recognized poorly by a model trained mostly on inland valleys. About 6% of California has a climate unlike anywhere the model learned from, and estimates there are least reliable.
